kid.question: What does the Lord promise the children of His people?

options.text: They will become great soldiers
They will travel to Egypt
They will build new ships
They will learn from Him

kid.explanation: The children will be taught of the Lord, and their peace will be great.

kid.question: What does Isaiah say the people will be established in?

options.text: Owning many strong weapons
Doing what is right
Making friends with rulers
Building tall city walls

kid.explanation: The promise begins with being established in righteousness, followed by freedom from oppression and terror.

kid.question: What will happen to weapons made against the Lord's servants?

options.text: They will become stronger
They will be traded
They will be hidden
They will not succeed

kid.explanation: The Lord promises that no weapon formed against His servants will prosper.

kid.question: Who is invited to come to the waters?

options.text: Everyone who brings silver
Everyone who is thirsty
People who own farmland
People who command armies

kid.explanation: The invitation is to everyone who thirsts, including those who have no money.

kid.question: What does the Lord tell people to do to receive what is good?

options.text: Work longer for money
Listen carefully to Him
Travel farther for food
Ask rulers for permission

kid.explanation: The Lord contrasts unsatisfying purchases with diligently listening to Him and receiving what is good.

kid.question: What does the Lord offer those who come and hear Him?

options.text: A lasting covenant
A royal position
A trading agreement
A secret message

kid.explanation: The Lord says their souls will live and promises an everlasting covenant.

kid.question: When does Isaiah tell people to seek the Lord?

options.text: After they become rich
Before the next harvest
While He is near
During the king's celebration

kid.explanation: The people are told to seek the Lord while He may be found and call upon Him while He is near.

kid.question: What should someone doing wrong do to receive the Lord's mercy?

options.text: Turn back to Him
Hide their mistakes carefully
Blame another person first
Wait for others to change

kid.explanation: The wicked should forsake their ways and return to the Lord, who will have mercy and abundantly pardon.

kid.question: What picture describes how God's ways compare with ours?

options.text: Heaven high above earth
A river beside a road
A tent beside a house
A seed beneath the ground

kid.explanation: As the heavens are higher than the earth, God's ways and thoughts are higher than ours.

kid.question: How does Isaiah describe the people's journey out?

options.text: With fear and anger
With pride and boasting
With joy and peace
With grief and shame

kid.explanation: Isaiah says they will go out with joy and be led forth with peace, while creation joins the celebration.

high-school.question: What kind of security do these verses connect with the Lord's teaching?

options.text: Peace rooted in righteousness
Peace purchased through tribute
Safety secured by foreign troops
Safety maintained through secrecy

high-school.explanation: The children are taught by the Lord and have great peace; the people are established in righteousness and freed from fear.

high-school.question: How does the reference to the weapon-maker support the assurance that follows?

options.text: The Creator's authority extends over instruments of destruction
The Creator asks the weapon-maker to abandon his craft
The smith's skill becomes the source of divine righteousness
The smith's work proves the people's enemies cannot gather

high-school.explanation: God created the smith and destroyer; the following assurance places threats under His greater authority.

high-school.question: What contrast is developed through buying and eating?

options.text: Expensive divine nourishment versus cheap food from neighboring nations
Scarce water for travelers versus abundant water for wealthy citizens
Free divine nourishment versus costly things that fail to satisfy
Ordinary bread for farmers versus forbidden bread for foreign rulers

high-school.explanation: The invitation includes those without money and contrasts God's good gifts with expenditures that do not satisfy.

high-school.question: Why are hearing and coming linked to the covenant promise?

options.text: Receiving a covenant removes the need to hear again
Responding to the Lord brings life and covenant relationship
Traveling to a distant city earns an inherited title
Listening to a king replaces responding to the Lord

high-school.explanation: The commands to hear and come are followed by the promise that the soul will live and receive an everlasting covenant.

high-school.question: How does the passage widen the scope of God's promise?

options.text: It restricts the covenant to a familiar royal household
It draws previously unfamiliar nations toward His people
It sends every foreign nation away from the gathering
It makes foreign armies the authors of divine glory

high-school.explanation: A witness and leader to the people is followed by nations formerly unknown coming because the Lord has glorified His people.

high-school.question: Which response does the invitation to seek the Lord require?

options.text: Abandon wrong ways and return for mercy
Keep familiar ways and request greater prosperity
Avoid past enemies and postpone personal repentance
Find a human ruler and offer public praise

high-school.explanation: Seeking the Lord includes forsaking wicked ways and unrighteous thoughts, then returning to receive mercy and pardon.

high-school.question: What does the comparison with heaven teach about God's thoughts?

options.text: They change with the movement of the stars
They depend on people's ability to predict weather
They exceed the measure of human understanding
They remain identical to the thoughts of prophets

high-school.explanation: Heaven's height over the earth illustrates the greater height of divine ways and thoughts over human ones.

high-school.question: What feature of rain explains the comparison with God's word?

options.text: It always arrives on a predictable schedule
It achieves a purpose by producing growth
It falls only on fields already planted
It returns before providing anything for people

high-school.explanation: Rain waters the earth and produces seed and bread; God's word likewise accomplishes the purpose for which He sends it.

high-school.question: How does the promise about God's word support the joyful departure?

options.text: His private message replaces the need for travel
His spoken warning demands silence during departure
His unfulfilled promise requires the people to wait
His effective promise gives grounds for hope

high-school.explanation: The word accomplishes God's purpose; the next verse pictures the promised departure marked by joy and peace.

high-school.question: What connects the promise of righteousness with the invitation to the waters?

options.text: Both present rewards purchased through successful labor
Both restrict help to people with royal ancestry
Both make physical weapons a requirement for salvation
Both present benefits received from the Lord

high-school.explanation: Righteousness is of the Lord, and the waters are offered without money, emphasizing divine provision in both passages.

expert.question: What best describes the movement of the restoration promises?

options.text: From public accusation to a command for military revenge
From fortified borders to the abolition of all judgment
From unrighteous children to dependence on foreign smiths
From instructed children to security against public accusation

expert.explanation: Teaching and peace lead into establishment in righteousness and assurances concerning weapons and accusing tongues.

expert.question: What does the smith-and-destroyer claim contribute to the argument?

options.text: Threatening agents remain within the Creator's larger sovereignty
Threatening agents possess powers outside the Creator's authority
The servants' righteousness results from mastery of weapon production
The servants' security depends on replacing every hostile craftsman

expert.explanation: Creation of the smith and destroyer grounds the declaration that weapons and accusations will not defeat God's servants.

expert.question: What does the apparently commercial invitation undermine?

options.text: Access to divine nourishment as a function of wealth
Access to divine nourishment as a response to thirst
The distinction between water and agricultural products
The distinction between the speaker and the hearers

expert.explanation: Buying without money overturns ordinary payment as a condition; the following question challenges costly but unsatisfying expenditure.

expert.question: How does the passage reinterpret its food imagery?

options.text: Physical nourishment becomes a requirement for financing the royal court
Physical nourishment becomes a figure for hearing and covenant life
The soul's survival depends on accumulating ordinary commercial goods
The soul's delight requires replacing covenant with political command

expert.explanation: Eating what is good leads into inclining the ear, hearing, soul-life, and an everlasting covenant.

expert.question: Which development follows the mention of David's sure mercies?

options.text: The covenant horizon extends toward previously unknown nations
The covenant horizon contracts to David's immediate biological household
The promised mercies become payment for a foreign ruler
The promised mercies cancel the role of witness and leader

expert.explanation: The covenant and Davidic mercies are followed by witness and leadership imagery and the attraction of unfamiliar nations.

expert.question: How are urgency and pardon combined in the invitation?

options.text: Seek later and preserve familiar habits to receive abundant mercy
Seek now and abandon wrongdoing to receive abundant mercy
Seek now because mercy is limited to the already righteous
Seek later because pardon depends on a future political leader

expert.explanation: While He is near makes the invitation urgent; forsaking wicked ways and returning are answered by abundant pardon.

expert.question: What does the immediate context suggest about the higher-ways claim?

options.text: Divine thought removes any need for ethical change
Divine pardon exceeds ordinary expectations of mercy
Heaven's height supplies a timetable for the invitation
Heaven's distance makes returning to God impossible

expert.explanation: The claim follows the promise of abundant pardon, so God's greater ways help ground hope for mercy beyond human expectations.

expert.question: Which correspondence is essential to the rain-and-word analogy?

options.text: Descent followed by disappearance without any remaining effect
A return that occurs before the earth receives nourishment
Descent that produces its intended life-giving result
A return that depends on approval from the people

expert.explanation: Rain gives seed and bread instead of returning ineffectually; the word similarly accomplishes what God intends.

expert.question: How does the verse define the effectiveness of divine speech?

options.text: Agreement with the hearer's preferred outcome
Immediate fulfillment of every human request
Achievement of the sender's intended purpose
Independence from the sender after being spoken

expert.explanation: The word accomplishes what God pleases and prospers in the purpose for which He sent it.

expert.question: What does the personification of mountains and trees accomplish?

options.text: Creation replaces the people as the recipients of pardon
Creation explains the failure of the preceding divine word
Creation demonstrates that the departure is a military invasion
Creation participates in the joy of the people's departure

expert.explanation: Singing hills and clapping trees expand the joyful and peaceful departure into a scene of creation-wide celebration.
